title: Long-Term Investing
concept: Long-term investing means following an investment plan over several years while accepting that prices may rise and fall during shorter periods.
learningObjective: Understand why a long-term investment plan should not be judged only by its performance during one short period.
primaryMisconception: Investing should produce significant results quickly.
secondaryMisconceptions: A temporary decline means the long-term investment plan has failed.
Long-term investing means ignoring every change or warning sign.
keyTakeaway: Long-term investing requires patience and the ability to tolerate uncertainty.

screens.title: One Bad Year
screens.content: You plan for ten years. After one bad year, your portfolio drops below its starting value. Is the whole plan already broken?
screens.illustration: A ten-year road continues ahead while the Year 2 marker dips below the starting line.

screens.title: A Ten-Year Goal
screens.content: You invest a fictional Rs. 100,000 in a diversified portfolio for a goal ten years away.
screens.illustration: A Rs. 100,000 portfolio card connects to a goal marker at Year 10.

screens.title: The First Drop
screens.content: The portfolio rises in Year 1, then falls to Rs. 92,000 in Year 2. The goal is still eight years away.
screens.illustration: The value line rises to Rs. 105,000 and then drops below the starting value.

screens.title: Patience Needs Review
screens.content: You can react to every movement, ignore everything, or review whether the plan still fits before deciding.
screens.illustration: Three paths show emotional selling, blind holding, and thoughtful review.

screens.title: How Should One Year Be Judged?
screens.question: After the Year 2 decline, which response uses the long-term plan most effectively?

options.text: Sell immediately because the plan failed
options.response: One difficult year may be too little information to judge a ten-year plan.

options.text: Ignore every warning and never review
options.response: Patience matters, but long-term investing still requires thoughtful review.

options.text: Review the goal and investment, then decide
options.response: Correct. This separates short-term emotion from genuine changes that may require action.

options.text: Expect a large profit next year
options.response: A recovery may occur, but future returns cannot be predicted or guaranteed.

config.outcomeExplanation: The fictional portfolio ends at Rs. 165,000 after several declines and recoveries. The lesson is not that holding always wins. It is that one short period may be insufficient to judge a long-term plan, and patience should be combined with regular review.

screens.title: Judge the Plan Over the Right Period
screens.content: You followed a portfolio through gains, declines, and recoveries. Long-term investing means using a multi-year plan instead of judging everything by one short period. It requires patience, but not blind holding. Goals, time horizon, fees, risk, and investment quality still need review. A temporary decline may recover, remain low, or worsen. The point is to make evidence-based decisions rather than expecting quick results or reacting only to recent price movement.
screens.simpleSummary: Use the full plan, not one bad year, to guide decisions.
screens.illustration: A ten-year chart shows declines inside a longer journey, with review checkpoints placed at Years 2, 5, and 8.

screens.title: A Goal Still Seven Years Away
screens.content: Sana’s fictional retirement portfolio falls during one year, but her goal remains seven years away. She reviews its fees, diversification, and quality before deciding. She does not assume recovery, but she also does not judge the entire plan by one decline.
screens.illustration: A retirement goal sits seven years ahead while Sana checks a review list beside a temporary decline.

The mission uses PKR, a diversified portfolio, ten-year goals, and familiar adult investment decisions in Pakistan.
The learner follows ten years of results and makes evidence-based decisions at three difficult points.
The quiz addresses quick results, temporary declines, guaranteed recovery, and blind holding.
